machine: Apple M3 Pro, 18 GB unified memory, 11 CPU cores (5P+6E), macOS 26.5.2
notes: env-steps/s = control steps per second summed over all environments (physics substeps / frame-skip included). MLX: median of 5 timing windows, random actions generated on GPU, full mx.eval every step, auto-reset included, mx.compile on the physics step. MuJoCo: Gymnasium-style models written inline (InvertedPendulum-like cartpole, timestep 0.02 frame_skip 2; HalfCheetah-like planar model, timestep 0.01 frame_skip 5), plain Python mj_step loop with random ctrl, then one process per core (11 processes, spawn, warm). IMPORTANT CAVEAT: this is not an apples-to-apples physics comparison. MacGym's MLX tasks use our own simplified 2D planar maximal-coordinate dynamics (capsule bodies, penalty ground contact, few substeps), while MuJoCo solves full 3D generalized-coordinate dynamics with a constraint-based contact solver. The MuJoCo numbers also include Python loop overhead per step. The MLX walker task is compared against the MuJoCo half-cheetah as the nearest planar locomotion model. Read the speedups as 'how much RL experience per second this laptop can generate for these tasks', not as 'MLX is X times faster than MuJoCo at the same physics'. Numbers vary run to run (roughly +/-30% observed on the GPU side) because the laptop was not otherwise idle during the hackathon (other training jobs share the GPU); MuJoCo multi-process uses all P and E cores. MLX tasks measured via: {'cartpole': 'macgym.envs', 'walker': 'macgym.envs', 'cheetah': 'macgym.envs'}. mlx 0.32.4, mujoco 4.0.1, Python 3.13.12.
